hint: rim where the front of the frontal lobe turns under toward the orbit
summary: The frontomarginal gyrus and sulcus lie at the anterior end of the frontal lobe, where the lateral surface rolls onto the orbital surface. They are located lateral and ventral to the transverse frontopolar gyri and form part of anterior prefrontal cortex. The Destrieux atlas labels the gyrus and sulcus together as a single parcel. No function has been assigned to this gyrus separately from the surrounding frontopolar cortex.
where: The gyrus and sulcus occupy the anterior margin of the frontal lobe, at the transition from the lateral to the orbital surface. They lie just lateral and ventral to the transverse frontopolar gyri. They are seen best in an anterolateral or inferior view.
does: The gyrus belongs to anterior prefrontal cortex and has no distinct function attributed to it. Lateral frontopolar cortex has been associated with maintaining a main goal while a subgoal is carried out and with prospective memory. Imaging rarely resolves these effects to this single gyrus.
connects: It shares the reciprocal connections of anterior prefrontal cortex with dorsolateral and orbital prefrontal cortex and with the mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus.
clinical: Isolated damage to this gyrus is rare. Frontopolar injury in general produces impaired multitasking and planning with preservation of basic intelligence. The sulcus serves chiefly as a landmark on maps of the anterior frontal surface.
remember: Marginal denotes an edge: this gyrus lies on the margin of the frontal pole.
facts: It is labeled G_and_S_frontomargin in the Destrieux atlas, gyrus and sulcus together.
It lies between the frontal pole and the orbital surface.
It is part of the prefrontal cortex, not of the motor frontal lobe.

quiz.q: The small gyrus and sulcus at the margin where the front of the frontal lobe curves onto the orbital surface, lateral to the short transverse gyri at the tip.
The Destrieux label G_and_S_frontomargin names which gyrus?

hint: lowest ridge on the lateral surface of the rear visual lobe
summary: The inferior occipital gyrus is the lowest gyrus on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe. It lies below the middle occipital gyrus, from which it is separated by the inferior occipital sulcus, and it extends toward the preoccipital notch. It contains ventral extrastriate visual areas that process shape, and the occipital face area is usually located on or beside it. It receives input from V1 and V2 and projects forward along the ventral visual stream.
where: The gyrus forms the inferior margin of the lateral occipital surface, below the middle occipital gyrus. It runs toward the preoccipital notch and merges with the inferior temporal region. It is seen best in a lateral or inferior view.
does: It contains ventral extrastriate visual areas involved in shape processing. The occipital face area, an early face-selective region, lies on or near it, upstream of the fusiform face area. It also borders the lateral occipital complex, which responds to object shape.
connects: It receives visual input from V1 and V2 and projects forward along the ventral visual stream to the fusiform and inferior temporal gyri.
clinical: Damage to the right inferior occipital region together with the fusiform gyrus can produce apperceptive prosopagnosia, in which faces are not perceived as faces. Lesions of ventral occipital cortex can also produce visual form agnosia.
remember: The inferior occipital gyrus is the first stage of the face-processing route, lying below the middle occipital gyrus.
facts: The occipital face area is usually placed on or beside it.
It is separated from the middle occipital gyrus by the inferior occipital sulcus.
It is a ventral stream, or what pathway, region.

quiz.q: The gyrus at the lower edge of the lateral occipital surface that is the usual site of the occipital face area.
Which lateral occipital gyrus lies below the middle occipital gyrus, next to the preoccipital notch?

hint: top-medial cortex where the central sulcus ends, leg and bladder
summary: The paracentral lobule is the region of the medial hemispheric surface where the precentral and postcentral gyri continue over the superior margin. It is bounded anteriorly by the paracentral sulcus, posteriorly by the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus and inferiorly by the cingulate sulcus. Its anterior part is motor and its posterior part is sensory, and together they represent the contralateral foot and lower leg. The lobule also participates in voluntary control of the bladder and bowel.
where: The lobule lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere, where the precentral and postcentral gyri curve over the top and meet. The paracentral sulcus bounds it in front, the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus behind and the cingulate sulcus below. A sagittal or medial view shows it best.
does: The anterior part is motor cortex and the posterior part is somatosensory cortex, so the lobule represents the contralateral foot, lower leg and pelvic floor. This region takes part in voluntary control of bladder and bowel function.
connects: The motor part gives rise to corticospinal fibers for the leg and receives input from the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus. The sensory part receives lower limb input through the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus.
clinical: An anterior cerebral artery stroke damages this lobule and produces contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, often with urinary incontinence. Parasagittal meningiomas can compress it and cause progressive leg weakness.
remember: The homunculus folds over the superior margin, so the foot representation lies in the medial paracentral lobule.
facts: It is the medial extension of the precentral and postcentral gyri.
Its blood supply comes from the anterior cerebral artery.
The marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus marks its posterior border.

quiz.q: The lobule on the medial surface formed by the continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri over the top of the hemisphere.
An anterior cerebral artery stroke causes contralateral leg weakness and bladder incontinence by damaging this medial lobule.

hint: lid over the lower insula where pre and postcentral gyri meet
summary: The subcentral gyrus is a narrow gyrus at the inferior end of the central sulcus, where the lower ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri join just above the lateral sulcus. It forms part of the operculum that covers the insula and is also called the central or rolandic operculum. It contains the most inferior part of the sensorimotor strip, which represents the mouth, tongue, pharynx and larynx. It participates in swallowing, chewing and control of the vocal tract.
where: The gyrus lies at the lower end of the central sulcus, joining the bottom of the precentral and postcentral gyri just above the lateral sulcus. It forms part of the operculum that covers the insula. Its sulci are shallow and variable.
does: It contains the lowest part of the sensorimotor strip, representing the mouth, tongue, pharynx and larynx. It lies near secondary somatosensory and gustatory cortex. It takes part in swallowing, chewing and control of the vocal tract.
connects: It is connected with ventral sensorimotor cortex, the adjacent frontal and parietal opercula and the posterior insula.
clinical: Bilateral lesions of the opercular region cause Foix-Chavany-Marie syndrome, with loss of voluntary movement of the face, tongue and pharynx and preservation of automatic and reflex movements. Opercular seizures can produce oral automatisms and taste sensations.
remember: Operculum means lid: this gyrus lies below the central sulcus and above the insula, covering the insula.
facts: It is also called the central operculum or rolandic operculum.
It lies directly under the lower end of the central sulcus.
Bilateral damage gives the anterior opercular, or Foix-Chavany-Marie, syndrome.

quiz.q: The strip of cortex that joins the lower ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri and forms the lid over the posterior insula.
Bilateral lesions here cause loss of voluntary face, tongue and pharynx movement with preserved automatic movement (Foix-Chavany-Marie).

hint: short folds at the very tip of the frontal lobe
summary: The transverse frontopolar gyri and sulci are the short folds at the anterior tip of the frontal lobe, which together form the frontal pole. They extend onto the medial, lateral and inferior surfaces at the tip and correspond to Brodmann area 10, or anterior prefrontal cortex. This region is proportionally larger in humans than in other apes. It is associated with branching, in which a main goal is held while a subgoal is carried out, and with prospective memory.
where: The gyri and sulci form the anterior tip of the frontal lobe, the frontal pole, and extend onto its medial, lateral and inferior surfaces. The pole is seen best in front-on or sagittal views.
does: This region is Brodmann area 10, anterior prefrontal cortex. It is associated with branching, the maintenance of a main goal while a subgoal is carried out, and with prospective memory and the tracking of multiple tasks. Findings vary, and its precise function remains debated.
connects: It is connected with dorsolateral and orbital prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex and the mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus, and it receives very little direct sensory input.
clinical: Damage to the frontal pole can leave intelligence test scores intact while multitasking, planning and remembering to carry out later intentions fail. The pole is vulnerable in frontal pole tumors and in trauma to the front of the skull.
remember: Pole means tip: these short gyri form the most anterior cortex, immediately behind the front of the skull.
facts: It corresponds to Brodmann area 10.
It is the most anterior cortex of the frontal lobe.
It is relatively larger in humans than in other apes.

quiz.q: The short transverse folds at the very anterior tip of the frontal lobe, the front of the brain.
The part of the frontal lobe corresponding to Brodmann area 10, linked to holding a main goal while carrying out a subgoal.

hint: medial cortex wrapping the front of the corpus callosum
summary: The anterior cingulate gyrus is the most anterior segment of the cingulate gyrus on the medial hemispheric surface. It curves around the genu of the corpus callosum, separated from it by the callosal sulcus, and corresponds mainly to the pregenual cingulate. It is connected with the amygdala, hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex and anterior insula. It links emotion with autonomic control, evaluating the emotional significance of events and regulating heart rate and arousal.
where: The segment lies on the medial surface, curving around the genu of the corpus callosum and separated from it by the callosal sulcus. It continues below into the subcallosal gyrus and behind into the anterior midcingulate part. A midsagittal view shows it best.
does: It corresponds mainly to the pregenual part of the cingulate. It links emotion with autonomic control, evaluating the emotional significance of events and regulating heart rate and arousal. The wider anterior cingulate cortex also supports error and conflict monitoring, but this function is usually assigned to the more posterior midcingulate part.
connects: It is connected with the amygdala, hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex and anterior insula, and it projects to autonomic brainstem centers.
clinical: Stereotactic cingulotomy in this region has been used for refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder and severe chronic pain. Bilateral damage to the medial frontal region can produce akinetic mutism.
remember: Anterior denotes the segment that hugs the front end of the corpus callosum, the genu.
facts: It is the front-most of five Destrieux cingulate divisions.
It lies above the callosal sulcus and below the cingulate sulcus.
It surrounds the genu of the corpus callosum.

quiz.q: The segment of the cingulate gyrus that curves around the genu of the corpus callosum, the most anterior of the cingulate divisions.
Which cingulate segment lies in front of the anterior midcingulate part and above the subcallosal area?

hint: medial strip over the front half of the callosal body
summary: The anterior midcingulate gyrus is the middle-anterior part of the cingulate gyrus, lying above the anterior half of the body of the corpus callosum on the medial surface. It is bounded in front by the anterior cingulate part and behind by the posterior midcingulate part, and it follows a cingulate sulcus that often splits into two parallel sulci. It is the cognitive control division of the cingulate and contains the rostral cingulate motor area in the banks of the cingulate sulcus. It is active during conflict, response selection, error detection, effort and the affective dimension of pain.
where: The segment lies above the anterior half of the body of the corpus callosum on the medial surface. It follows the cingulate sulcus, which often splits into two parallel sulci here. It is bounded in front by the anterior cingulate part and behind by the posterior midcingulate part.
does: It forms the cognitive control division of the cingulate. It is active during conflict, response selection, error detection, effort and the affective dimension of pain. It also contains the rostral cingulate motor area in the banks of the cingulate sulcus.
connects: It is connected with lateral prefrontal cortex, the supplementary motor area, the anterior insula and the basal ganglia. Through the cingulate motor areas it sends some fibers to the spinal cord and motor cortex.
clinical: Bilateral damage to medial frontal cortex including this region causes akinetic mutism, with preserved wakefulness but little movement or speech. Lesions for anterior cingulotomy are placed near this region for intractable pain.
remember: Midcingulate denotes the middle of the callosal body, and the anterior half is the cognitive division.
facts: It is labeled G_and_S_cingul-Mid-Ant in the Destrieux atlas.
The rostral cingulate motor area lies in the banks of its sulcus.
It overlies the anterior half of the corpus callosum body.

quiz.q: The cingulate segment over the anterior half of the body of the corpus callosum, behind the pregenual part and in front of the part level with the central sulcus.
The cingulate segment whose sulcal banks hold the rostral cingulate motor area.

hint: medial strip over the back half of the callosal body
summary: The posterior midcingulate gyrus is the middle-posterior part of the cingulate gyrus, lying above the posterior half of the body of the corpus callosum. It lies roughly beneath the end of the central sulcus and the paracentral lobule, between the anterior midcingulate part and the dorsal posterior cingulate part. It is more sensorimotor than the anterior midcingulate part and contains the caudal cingulate motor area. It takes part in orienting the body and eyes to salient events and in skeletomotor control.
where: The segment lies above the posterior half of the body of the corpus callosum. It is located roughly beneath the end of the central sulcus and the paracentral lobule. It is bounded in front by the anterior midcingulate part and behind by the dorsal posterior cingulate part.
does: It is more sensorimotor than the anterior midcingulate part. It contains the caudal cingulate motor area and takes part in orienting the body and eyes to salient events and in skeletomotor control. It is also activated by pain, mainly in its motor and orienting aspects.
connects: Through the caudal cingulate motor area it is connected with primary and supplementary motor cortex, parietal cortex and the spinal cord.
clinical: Seizures arising in the cingulate can cause complex motor automatisms and hypermotor behavior. This segment is rarely damaged in isolation.
remember: The posterior half of the callosal body, beneath the paracentral lobule, is the motor division of the cingulate.
facts: It is labeled G_and_S_cingul-Mid-Post in the Destrieux atlas.
The caudal cingulate motor area lies here.
It lies below the paracentral lobule.

quiz.q: The cingulate segment above the posterior half of the callosal body, beneath the paracentral lobule and in front of the dorsal posterior part.
The cingulate segment holding the caudal cingulate motor area, with direct projections to the spinal cord.

hint: medial strip arching over the back end of the callosum
summary: The dorsal posterior cingulate gyrus is the posterior-dorsal part of the cingulate gyrus, arching over the splenium of the corpus callosum on the medial surface. It lies behind the posterior midcingulate part and in front of the isthmus, with the precuneus above it. It is joined to the precuneus, hippocampal formation and anterior thalamus through the cingulum bundle. It is a major hub of the default mode network, active at rest and during autobiographical memory, self-reference and spatial memory.
where: The segment arches over the splenium of the corpus callosum on the medial surface. It lies behind the posterior midcingulate part and in front of the isthmus. The marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus marks its upper border, and the precuneus lies above it.
does: It is a major hub of the default mode network, active at rest and during autobiographical memory, self-reference and spatial memory. It also contributes to shifting attention between internal thought and external tasks. These roles are inferred mainly from imaging.
connects: It is connected with the precuneus, hippocampal formation and anterior thalamus through the cingulum bundle, and with medial prefrontal cortex.
clinical: The posterior cingulate and neighboring precuneus are among the first regions to show reduced metabolism on FDG-PET in early Alzheimer disease. Amyloid also accumulates here early.
remember: Dorsal posterior denotes the arch over the back end of the callosum, with the isthmus below it.
facts: It is labeled G_cingul-Post-dorsal in the Destrieux atlas.
It is part of the default mode network.
It lies above the splenium of the corpus callosum.

quiz.q: The segment of the cingulate gyrus that arches above the splenium, between the posterior midcingulate part and the isthmus.
The cingulate segment bounded above by the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus, and below by the isthmus that wraps around the splenium.

hint: narrow neck of medial cortex curling round the splenium
summary: The ventral posterior cingulate gyrus, or isthmus of the cingulate gyrus, is a narrow neck of cortex that wraps behind and beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. It connects the cingulate gyrus above with the parahippocampal gyrus below and corresponds to retrosplenial cortex, Brodmann areas 29 and 30. It is connected with the hippocampal formation, parahippocampal gyrus, anterior thalamus and posterior parietal cortex. It supports scene processing, spatial memory and navigation.
where: The isthmus is a narrow neck of cortex wrapping behind and under the splenium of the corpus callosum. It connects the cingulate gyrus above with the parahippocampal gyrus below. It is seen in the medial view, near the junction of the parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci.
does: It corresponds to retrosplenial cortex, Brodmann areas 29 and 30. It supports scene processing, spatial memory and navigation, in particular the use of landmarks for orientation. It also takes part in episodic memory retrieval together with the hippocampus.
connects: It is connected with the hippocampal formation, parahippocampal gyrus, anterior thalamus and posterior parietal cortex, and forms part of the extended Papez circuit.
clinical: Retrosplenial lesions can cause topographical disorientation, in which a person recognizes landmarks but cannot use them to navigate, and a rare form of amnesia. This region shows early metabolic decline in Alzheimer disease.
remember: Isthmus means narrow neck: this segment forms the bridge from the cingulate gyrus to the parahippocampal gyrus.
facts: It corresponds to retrosplenial cortex.
It connects the cingulate and parahippocampal gyri.
It wraps around the splenium.

quiz.q: The narrow neck of cortex that curves around the splenium and joins the cingulate gyrus to the parahippocampal gyrus.
Lesions of this retrosplenial cortex cause topographical disorientation, with landmarks recognized but not used for navigation.

hint: medial rear cortex above the calcarine sulcus
summary: The cuneus is a wedge-shaped region of the medial occipital surface, lying between the parieto-occipital sulcus in front and the calcarine sulcus below. Its lower part lines the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus, which is primary visual cortex, V1, and represents the contralateral lower visual field. Its upper part contains V2, V3 and dorsal stream visual areas. It receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the optic radiations and projects forward to the dorsal visual stream.
where: The cuneus is a wedge of the medial occipital surface lying between the parieto-occipital sulcus in front and the calcarine sulcus below. Its point faces the calcarine sulcus. The medial view shows it best.
does: Its lower part lines the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus, which is V1 and represents the lower visual field of the opposite side. Its upper part holds V2, V3 and dorsal stream visual areas. It also shows attention and working memory effects in imaging.
connects: It receives from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the optic radiations, whose superior fibers pass through the parietal lobe, and projects forward to the dorsal visual stream.
clinical: A lesion confined to the cuneus produces a contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia, the pie on the floor. Complete V1 damage produces homonymous hemianopia, with macular sparing if the occipital pole is spared.
remember: Cuneus means wedge in Latin; the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus represents the lower visual field.
facts: Cuneus means wedge in Latin.
A lesion gives an inferior quadrantanopia on the opposite side.
It lies above the calcarine sulcus.

quiz.q: The wedge-shaped gyrus on the medial occipital surface between the parieto-occipital sulcus and the calcarine sulcus.
A lesion confined to this gyrus causes a contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia.

aliases: opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
hint: frontal lid over the insula, just ahead of the lower precentral groove
summary: The pars opercularis is the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus and corresponds to Brodmann area 44. It lies directly in front of the inferior precentral sulcus and behind the anterior ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus, and it forms part of the frontal operculum covering the insula. In the left hemisphere it constitutes the posterior part of Broca's area. It is connected with ventral premotor cortex, the inferior parietal lobule and posterior temporal cortex through the arcuate and superior longitudinal fasciculi.
where: The gyrus lies directly in front of the inferior precentral sulcus and behind the anterior ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus. It forms part of the frontal operculum covering the insula. A lateral view shows it best.
does: It is Brodmann area 44. In the left hemisphere it forms the posterior part of Broca's area, although the gyrus itself is an anatomical structure defined by its sulcal borders. It lies adjacent to ventral premotor cortex and is related to motor planning of the mouth and hand.
connects: It is connected with ventral premotor cortex, the inferior parietal lobule and posterior temporal cortex through the arcuate fasciculus and the superior longitudinal fasciculus.
clinical: Left-sided lesions here contribute to the damage in Broca's aphasia. Its borders are used as landmarks for language mapping in neurosurgery.
remember: Opercularis derives from operculum, meaning lid: this part of the inferior frontal gyrus covers the insula.
facts: It is the posterior of the three parts of the inferior frontal gyrus.
It corresponds to Brodmann area 44.
It lies in front of the inferior precentral sulcus.

quiz.q: The part of the inferior frontal gyrus directly in front of the inferior precentral sulcus and behind the anterior ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus.
The inferior frontal part named for the lid, or operculum, it forms over the insula.

aliases: orbital part of the inferior frontal gyrus
hint: front-lower frontal convolution below the horizontal ramus
summary: The pars orbitalis is the anterior and inferior part of the inferior frontal gyrus and corresponds to Brodmann area 47. It lies below the anterior horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus and extends onto the orbital surface near the lateral orbital sulcus. In the left hemisphere it takes part in controlled semantic retrieval, the selection of a meaning when several compete. It is connected with the anterior temporal lobe through the uncinate fasciculus and with orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
where: The gyrus lies below the anterior horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus and extends onto the orbital surface near the lateral orbital sulcus. It is seen best from a lateral or inferolateral view.
does: It corresponds to Brodmann area 47. In the left hemisphere it takes part in controlled semantic retrieval, selecting a meaning when several compete. In the right hemisphere it is related to response inhibition. It is not part of Broca's area in the classic definition.
connects: It is connected with the anterior temporal lobe through the uncinate fasciculus and with orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
clinical: Left ventrolateral lesions impair selection among competing semantic candidates, producing word retrieval difficulty without the nonfluent speech of Broca's aphasia.
remember: Orbitalis denotes the part that dips toward the orbit: the anterior and inferior third of the inferior frontal gyrus.
facts: It corresponds to Brodmann area 47.
It lies below the anterior horizontal ramus.
It is the most anterior and inferior part of the inferior frontal gyrus.

quiz.q: The part of the inferior frontal gyrus that lies below the anterior horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus and extends toward the orbital surface.
The part of the inferior frontal gyrus corresponding to Brodmann area 47.

aliases: triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
hint: wedge-shaped frontal fold between the two ascending rami
summary: The pars triangularis is the triangular middle part of the inferior frontal gyrus and corresponds to Brodmann area 45. It lies between the anterior horizontal ramus below and the anterior ascending ramus behind, so that its apex points into the lateral sulcus. It is located in front of the pars opercularis and above the pars orbitalis. In the left hemisphere it forms the anterior part of Broca's area and contributes to semantic and syntactic selection.
where: The gyrus lies between the anterior horizontal ramus below and the anterior ascending ramus behind, so its apex points into the lateral sulcus. It is in front of the pars opercularis and above the pars orbitalis. A lateral view shows it best.
does: It corresponds to Brodmann area 45. In the left hemisphere it forms the anterior part of Broca's area and contributes to semantic and syntactic selection. The gyrus is often larger on the left, although this varies between individuals.
connects: It is connected with posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex through the arcuate fasciculus and with the anterior temporal lobe through the extreme capsule fiber system.
clinical: Left-sided damage involving this gyrus contributes to Broca's aphasia. Its edges are used as landmarks in surgical language mapping.
remember: Triangularis is the triangle lying between the two anterior rami of the lateral sulcus.
facts: It corresponds to Brodmann area 45.
It is the middle of the three parts of the inferior frontal gyrus.
It is bounded by the two anterior rami of the lateral sulcus.

quiz.q: The triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus between the two anterior rami of the lateral sulcus.
The part of the inferior frontal gyrus corresponding to Brodmann area 45, in front of the opercular part.

hint: broad lateral ridge between two long grooves, ahead of the motor strip
summary: The middle frontal gyrus is the broad gyrus of the lateral frontal convexity, lying between the superior frontal sulcus above and the inferior frontal sulcus below. It extends from the frontal pole back to the precentral gyrus. Its anterior and middle parts constitute dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports working memory and planning. Its posterior end, near the precentral sulcus, contains the frontal eye field, which drives voluntary saccades.
where: The gyrus lies on the lateral frontal convexity between the superior frontal sulcus above and the inferior frontal sulcus below. It runs from the frontal pole back to the precentral gyrus. A lateral view shows it best.
does: Its anterior and middle parts are dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports working memory and planning. Its posterior end, close to the precentral sulcus, contains the frontal eye field, which drives voluntary saccades. The exact boundary of the frontal eye field is variable.
connects: It is connected with parietal cortex through the superior longitudinal fasciculus and with the caudate nucleus, the mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus and the superior colliculus.
clinical: Dorsolateral lesions produce executive dysfunction. Destructive lesions of the frontal eye field deviate the eyes toward the side of the lesion, whereas an irritative focus deviates the eyes away from the lesion.
remember: F2: the middle frontal gyrus is the middle of three stacked longitudinal gyri on the lateral frontal lobe.
facts: It lies between the superior and inferior frontal sulci.
It is also called F2.
The frontal eye field lies at its posterior end, near the precentral sulcus.

quiz.q: The frontal gyrus bounded above by the superior frontal sulcus and below by the inferior frontal sulcus.
A destructive lesion at the posterior end of this gyrus, at the frontal eye field, makes the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion.

hint: top edge of the brain's front end, spilling onto the medial wall
summary: The superior frontal gyrus is the uppermost gyrus of the frontal lobe, lying above the superior frontal sulcus. It extends over the dorsal margin onto the medial surface as far as the cingulate sulcus. Its posterior medial portion contains the supplementary motor area and pre-supplementary motor area, which plan and sequence movement. Its dorsal and medial parts take part in working memory and self-referential thought.
where: The gyrus lies above the superior frontal sulcus and extends over the dorsal margin onto the medial surface, down to the cingulate sulcus. It is therefore visible from above and in a sagittal view. Its posterior medial part lies in front of the paracentral lobule.
does: Its posterior medial portion holds the supplementary motor area and pre-supplementary motor area, which plan and sequence movement. Its dorsal and medial parts take part in working memory and self-referential thought. The gyrus is large, and these functions map onto separate subregions.
connects: The supplementary motor area is connected with primary motor cortex, with the basal ganglia through the putamen and with the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus. The medial part connects with the anterior cingulate and the default mode network.
clinical: Surgical removal of the supplementary motor area causes supplementary motor area syndrome, with temporary contralateral akinesia and mutism that recovers over weeks. Medial frontal lesions can also cause an alien hand.
remember: F1: the uppermost of the stack of frontal gyri, running along the dorsal edge of the hemisphere.
facts: It is also called F1.
It extends onto the medial surface.
The supplementary motor area lies in its posterior medial part.

quiz.q: The gyrus along the top edge of the frontal lobe, continuing onto the medial surface above the cingulate sulcus.
Surgical removal of the posterior medial part of this gyrus causes transient contralateral akinesia and mutism that recovers over weeks.

hint: hindmost island cortex, behind the island's central groove
summary: The long insular gyrus is the posterior part of the insula, composed of the long gyri that lie behind the central sulcus of the insula. It is hidden beneath the frontoparietal and temporal opercula and slopes downward and backward from the insular apex. The posterior insula receives sensory input about pain, temperature, touch and internal body state from the ventral posterior and posterior thalamic nuclei. It is regarded as primary interoceptive cortex.
where: The posterior part of the insula is made up of the long gyri behind the central sulcus of the insula. It is hidden under the frontoparietal and temporal opercula and is seen only when the opercula are opened or in coronal MRI sections. It slopes downward and backward from the apex.
does: The posterior insula receives sensory input about pain, temperature, touch and internal body state and is regarded as primary interoceptive cortex. It also contributes to auditory and vestibular processing. Taste and emotional evaluation are functions of the anterior insula.
connects: It receives input from the ventral posterior and posterior thalamic nuclei and projects to the anterior insula, secondary somatosensory cortex and the amygdala.
clinical: Lesions and stimulation of the posterior insula alter pain and temperature perception, and insular damage can produce pain asymbolia, in which pain is recognized but does not appear to matter. Posterior insular stroke may mimic thalamic pain syndrome.
remember: Long gyri lie behind the central sulcus of the insula: long and posterior, short and anterior.
facts: There are usually two long gyri.
They lie behind the central sulcus of the insula.
The posterior insula handles pain and interoception.

quiz.q: The one or two long gyri of the insula lying behind the central sulcus of the insula.
The posterior part of the insula that receives thalamic pain and temperature input and is considered primary interoceptive cortex.

hint: fan of folds at the front of the island cortex
summary: The short insular gyri form the anterior part of the insula and consist of three gyri, the anterior, middle and posterior short gyri, that fan out from the insular apex. They lie in front of the central sulcus of the insula and are covered by the frontal operculum. The anterior insula integrates body state with emotion and is part of the salience network. It is connected with the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, orbitofrontal cortex and ventral striatum.
where: The three short gyri, anterior, middle and posterior, fan out from the insular apex in front of the central sulcus of the insula. They are covered by the frontal operculum. They are seen in an opened sylvian fissure or in coronal MRI.
does: The anterior insula integrates body state with emotion and is part of the salience network. It is involved in awareness of internal sensation, disgust, empathy for the pain of others and taste, with primary gustatory cortex in the anterior dorsal insula and the adjacent operculum. Some of these assignments remain debated.
connects: It is connected with the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, orbitofrontal cortex and ventral striatum, and it receives gustatory and visceral input from the thalamus.
clinical: Insular damage has been reported to abolish nicotine craving in some patients, although the evidence is limited. Bilateral anterior insula lesions can impair disgust recognition, and the region shows changes in addiction and anxiety disorders.
remember: Short gyri fan forward, three in number: short and anterior, long and posterior.
facts: There are usually three short gyri.
They lie in front of the central sulcus of the insula.
The anterior insula is part of the salience network.

quiz.q: The three short gyri that fan out from the insular apex, in front of the central sulcus of the insula.
The anterior insular gyri, covered by the frontal operculum and linked to the amygdala and anterior cingulate in the salience network.

hint: broad lateral ridge at the back of the brain, between two grooves
summary: The middle occipital gyrus is the largest gyrus on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, running between the superior occipital gyrus above and the inferior occipital gyrus below. It is bounded by the middle occipital sulcus and the lunate sulcus region and merges anteriorly with the parietal and temporal lobes. It includes the lateral occipital complex, which responds to object shape. Motion area V5, or MT, lies just anterior to it at the occipitotemporal junction.
where: The gyrus is the largest on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, between the superior occipital gyrus above and the inferior occipital gyrus below. It is bounded by the middle occipital sulcus and the lunate sulcus region and merges anteriorly with the parietal and temporal lobes. A lateral view shows it best.
does: It includes the lateral occipital complex, which responds to object shape regardless of whether the object is defined by lines, texture or motion. Motion area V5, or MT, lies just anterior to it at the occipitotemporal junction. It also contributes to visual attention and spatial processing.
connects: It receives input from V1, V2 and V3 and sends output to the ventral stream along the temporal lobe and to the dorsal stream in the parietal lobe.
clinical: Bilateral damage at the lateral occipitotemporal border near V5 can cause akinetopsia, or motion blindness. Lesions of the lateral occipital complex can produce visual form agnosia.
remember: The middle of the three lateral occipital gyri, stacked from top to bottom.
facts: It is the largest of the lateral occipital gyri.
It contains the lateral occipital complex.
V5 lies just anterior to it.

quiz.q: The largest gyrus on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, between the superior and inferior occipital gyri.
The occipital gyrus that holds the lateral occipital complex, which responds to object shape.

hint: topmost ridge on the lateral surface of the rear visual lobe
summary: The superior occipital gyrus is the most dorsal gyrus of the lateral occipital surface, continuing from the cuneus over the superior margin. It is bounded below by the superior occipital and transverse occipital sulci and lies next to the superior parietal lobule. It contains dorsal extrastriate visual areas such as V3A and V7, which have retinotopic maps. It receives input from V1 and V2 and feeds the dorsal visual stream to the posterior parietal cortex.
where: The gyrus is the most dorsal of the lateral occipital surface, continuing from the cuneus over the superior margin. It is bounded below by the superior occipital and transverse occipital sulci and lies next to the superior parietal lobule. A lateral or dorsal view shows it best.
does: It holds dorsal extrastriate visual areas such as V3A and V7, which have retinotopic maps and feed the dorsal visual stream. This supports visuospatial attention and the visual guidance of reaching.
connects: It receives input from V1 and V2 and sends visual information to posterior parietal cortex and the intraparietal areas along the dorsal stream, the where and how pathway.
clinical: Bilateral damage at the occipitoparietal border can cause Balint syndrome, with simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and ocular apraxia. Unilateral lesions can cause visual field defects in the lower field.
remember: The superior occipital gyrus lies at the dorsal edge of the occipital lobe and begins the where pathway.
facts: It is the dorsal-most lateral occipital gyrus.
It feeds the dorsal visual stream.
It is a continuation of the cuneus over the dorsal margin.

quiz.q: The most dorsal gyrus on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, a continuation of the cuneus over the dorsal margin.
Bilateral damage at this occipitoparietal border region causes Balint syndrome, with simultanagnosia and optic ataxia.

hint: long ridge on the underside of the temporal lobe, widest in the middle
summary: The fusiform gyrus is a long gyrus on the inferior surface of the temporal and occipital lobes, between the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally and the collateral sulcus medially. It is widest in the middle, tapers at both ends and is divided lengthwise by a shallow mid-fusiform sulcus. It is a high-level region of the ventral visual stream and receives input from earlier ventral visual areas and the occipital face area. Its mid-fusiform part, especially on the right, contains the fusiform face area, and a posterior left region corresponds to the visual word form area.
where: The gyrus lies on the inferior surface of the temporal and occipital lobes, between the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally and the collateral sulcus medially. It is widest in the middle and tapers at both ends, and a shallow mid-fusiform sulcus divides it lengthwise. An inferior view shows it best.
does: It is a high-level ventral stream region. The mid-fusiform part, especially on the right, contains the fusiform face area, which responds strongly to faces. On the left, a more posterior part is the visual word form area, and nearby regions process color and objects. Whether the face area is face-specific or reflects expertise remains debated.
connects: It receives input from earlier ventral visual areas and the occipital face area, and it projects to the anterior temporal lobe, the amygdala and prefrontal cortex.
clinical: Damage to the right or both fusiform gyri causes prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces. Damage near this gyrus can cause achromatopsia, loss of color vision, and left-sided damage can cause pure alexia.
remember: Fusiform means spindle-shaped: the gyrus is widest in the middle and pointed at both ends.
facts: Fusiform means spindle-shaped.
It lies between the occipitotemporal and collateral sulci.
It contains the fusiform face area.

quiz.q: The gyrus on the underside of the temporal lobe between the lateral occipitotemporal sulcus and the collateral sulcus, widest in the middle.
Damage to this gyrus, mainly on the right, causes prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces.

hint: medial rear cortex below the calcarine sulcus
summary: The lingual gyrus lies on the medial and inferior surface of the occipital lobe, below the calcarine sulcus and above the collateral sulcus. It is the counterpart of the cuneus on the opposite side of the calcarine sulcus and continues anteriorly into the parahippocampal gyrus. Its upper part lines the lower bank of the calcarine sulcus, which is V1 and represents the upper visual field. It receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus through Meyer's loop of the optic radiations and projects to the ventral visual stream.
where: The gyrus lies on the medial and inferior surface of the occipital lobe, below the calcarine sulcus and above the collateral sulcus. It is the counterpart of the cuneus across the calcarine sulcus and continues anteriorly into the parahippocampal gyrus. A medial view shows it best.
does: Its upper part lines the lower bank of the calcarine sulcus, which is V1 and represents the upper visual field. Ventral V2, V3 and VP lie on it, and nearby V4 is associated with color. It has also been linked to visual memory and word reading.
connects: It receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the temporal part of the optic radiations (Meyer's loop) and sends output to the ventral visual stream.
clinical: A lesion here produces a contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia, the pie in the sky. Bilateral lesions that include the fusiform gyrus can cause achromatopsia.
remember: Lingual means tongue-shaped; the lower bank of the calcarine sulcus represents the upper visual field.
facts: It lies below the calcarine sulcus.
A lesion gives a superior quadrantanopia on the opposite side.
It continues into the parahippocampal gyrus.

quiz.q: The occipital gyrus below the calcarine sulcus and above the collateral sulcus, continuing forward into the parahippocampal gyrus.
A lesion confined to this gyrus causes a contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia.

hint: medial temporal ridge hugging the hippocampus, ends in a hook
summary: The parahippocampal gyrus lies on the medial and inferior surface of the temporal lobe, between the collateral sulcus below and the hippocampal fissure above. Anteriorly it curls into the hook-shaped uncus, and posteriorly it continues into the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus and the lingual gyrus. Its anterior part contains the entorhinal and perirhinal cortex, which gather cortical input for the hippocampus. Its posterior part, parahippocampal cortex, processes scenes and spatial layout.
where: The gyrus lies on the medial and inferior surface of the temporal lobe, between the collateral sulcus below and the hippocampal fissure above. Anteriorly it curls into the hook-shaped uncus. Posteriorly it continues into the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus and the lingual gyrus. An inferior or medial view shows it best.
does: Its anterior part contains the entorhinal and perirhinal cortex, which gather cortical input for the hippocampus. Its posterior part, parahippocampal cortex, processes scenes and spatial layout and includes a scene-selective area known as the parahippocampal place area. The gyrus forms a gateway for memory formation.
connects: Entorhinal cortex gives rise to the perforant path into the dentate gyrus, and the subiculum sends return projections back through it. The gyrus is also connected with the cingulate gyrus through the cingulum.
clinical: Neurofibrillary tangles appear first in the entorhinal cortex in Alzheimer disease. Uncal herniation pushes the medial temporal lobe over the tentorial edge, compressing the oculomotor nerve and causing a dilated pupil.
remember: Para means beside: this is the gyrus beside the hippocampus, ending in the hook of the uncus.
facts: It lies between the collateral sulcus and the hippocampal fissure.
Its anterior end is the uncus.
It contains the entorhinal cortex.

quiz.q: The medial temporal gyrus along the hippocampus, separated from it by the hippocampal fissure, ending anteriorly in the uncus.
The gyrus whose anterior part contains the entorhinal cortex, origin of the perforant path.

hint: four folds on the underside of the frontal lobe above the eye socket
summary: The orbital gyri are the gyri on the inferior, or orbital, surface of the frontal lobe, lying on the roof of the orbit lateral to the olfactory sulcus. An H-shaped orbital sulcus divides them into four gyri: anterior, medial, posterior and lateral. They form much of the orbitofrontal cortex, which links sensory inputs such as taste, smell and vision with reward value and guides choice. They receive olfactory, gustatory, visual and visceral input and are connected with the amygdala and mediodorsal thalamus.
where: The gyri lie on the inferior (orbital) surface of the frontal lobe, on the roof of the orbit, lateral to the olfactory sulcus. An H-shaped orbital sulcus divides them into four: anterior, medial, posterior and lateral. An inferior view shows them best.
does: They form much of the orbitofrontal cortex, which links sensory inputs such as taste, smell and vision with reward value and guides choice. They also have a role in updating value after devaluation and in social and emotional behavior.
connects: They receive olfactory, gustatory, visual and visceral input and are connected with the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus and anterior cingulate cortex.
clinical: The orbital surface lies against the rough bony orbital roof and is a common site of contusions in head trauma. Damage can cause disinhibition, loss of social judgment and anosmia.
remember: The H-shaped orbital sulcus divides the orbital surface into four gyri.
facts: There are four orbital gyri.
They are separated by the H-shaped orbital sulcus.
They lie lateral to the olfactory sulcus.

quiz.q: The four gyri on the underside of the frontal lobe, lateral to the olfactory sulcus and divided by an H-shaped sulcus.
Gyri on the roof of the orbit that are often contused in head trauma, with disinhibition and loss of smell.

hint: inferior parietal arch over the end of the superior temporal sulcus
summary: The angular gyrus is the posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule and corresponds to Brodmann area 39. It arches over the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, behind the supramarginal gyrus and adjacent to the occipital lobe. It is a multimodal association region that takes part in reading, semantic integration, number processing and spatial cognition. It is also a core node of the default mode network.
where: The gyrus forms the posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, arching over the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus. It lies behind the supramarginal gyrus and next to the occipital lobe, and it corresponds to Brodmann area 39. A lateral view shows it best.
does: It is a multimodal association region that takes part in reading, semantic integration, number processing and spatial cognition. It is also a core node of the default mode network, active in memory retrieval and imagining the future. Its exact function remains debated.
connects: It is connected with the temporal lobe, the occipital lobe and prefrontal cortex through the superior longitudinal and arcuate fasciculi and the inferior fronto-occipital system.
clinical: Damage to the left angular gyrus produces Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right confusion. It can also cause alexia with agraphia.
remember: The angular gyrus caps the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, behind the supramarginal gyrus, which caps the lateral sulcus.
facts: It corresponds to Brodmann area 39.
It lies behind the supramarginal gyrus.
Left damage causes Gerstmann syndrome.

quiz.q: The gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule that arches over the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, behind the supramarginal gyrus.
Left-hemisphere damage here causes agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right confusion (Gerstmann syndrome).

hint: inferior parietal arch capping the end of the sylvian fissure
summary: The supramarginal gyrus is the anterior part of the inferior parietal lobule and corresponds to Brodmann area 40. It arches over the posterior end of the lateral sulcus, just behind the postcentral gyrus and in front of the angular gyrus. In the left hemisphere it supports phonological short-term storage and the planning of skilled actions with tools. In the right hemisphere it contributes to attention and body awareness.
where: The gyrus forms the anterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, arching over the posterior end of the lateral sulcus just behind the postcentral gyrus. It lies in front of the angular gyrus and corresponds to Brodmann area 40. A lateral view shows it best.
does: In the left hemisphere it supports phonological short-term storage, which holds speech sounds for repetition, and the planning of skilled actions with tools. In the right hemisphere it contributes to attention and body awareness. Its precise role in language remains debated.
connects: It receives input from somatosensory and auditory association cortex and is connected with the frontal lobe through the arcuate and superior longitudinal fasciculi.
clinical: Left-sided lesions can cause ideomotor apraxia, in which a patient cannot pantomime tool use to command despite normal strength, and may contribute to conduction aphasia. Right-sided damage can contribute to hemineglect.
remember: Supramarginal means above the margin: the gyrus caps the end of the lateral sulcus.
facts: It corresponds to Brodmann area 40.
It caps the posterior end of the lateral sulcus.
Left lesions can cause ideomotor apraxia.

quiz.q: The inferior parietal gyrus that caps the upper end of the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus, in front of the angular gyrus.
Left-hemisphere damage here can cause ideomotor apraxia, inability to pantomime tool use on command without weakness.

hint: cortex above the long groove on the top rear of the brain
summary: The superior parietal lobule is the part of the parietal lobe above the intraparietal sulcus, on the dorsal and lateral surface. It lies behind the postcentral gyrus, extends onto the medial side where it merges with the precuneus, and corresponds to Brodmann areas 5 and 7. It integrates somatosensory and visual information for the control of reaching and grasping, for spatial attention and for the body schema. It is a major component of the dorsal visual stream, the how pathway.
where: The lobule lies above the intraparietal sulcus on the dorsal and lateral surface of the parietal lobe, behind the postcentral gyrus. It extends onto the medial side, where it merges with the precuneus. It corresponds to Brodmann areas 5 and 7.
does: It integrates somatosensory and visual information for the control of reaching and grasping, and for spatial attention and the body schema. It is a major component of the dorsal visual stream, the how pathway.
connects: It receives input from somatosensory cortex and dorsal occipital areas and projects to premotor and motor cortex, mainly through the first branch of the superior longitudinal fasciculus.
clinical: Lesions cause optic ataxia, with misreaching under visual guidance, and astereognosis, in which objects cannot be recognized by touch. Bilateral damage contributes to Balint syndrome.
remember: Superior to the intraparietal sulcus: the parietal region for visually guided reaching.
facts: It lies above the intraparietal sulcus.
It corresponds to Brodmann areas 5 and 7.
Damage causes optic ataxia.

quiz.q: The part of the parietal lobe lying above the intraparietal sulcus, behind the postcentral gyrus.
A lesion here causes optic ataxia, misreaching to visual targets despite normal strength.

hint: ridge immediately behind the rolandic groove
summary: The postcentral gyrus is the gyrus of the parietal lobe immediately behind the central sulcus, running from the superior margin to the lateral sulcus. It is the primary somatosensory cortex, S1, and contains Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2. It receives input from the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei and projects to the superior parietal lobule, the supramarginal gyrus and the precentral gyrus. Each of its areas contains a map of the opposite side of the body.
where: The gyrus lies immediately behind the central sulcus, running from the superior margin to the lateral sulcus. It is bounded behind by the postcentral sulcus, which separates it from the superior and inferior parietal lobules. At the top it merges with the paracentral lobule and at the bottom with the subcentral gyrus.
does: It is the primary somatosensory cortex, S1. It forms the posterior wall of the central sulcus and the crown of the gyrus. Brodmann area 3 lies in the sulcal wall, area 1 on the crown and area 2 at the back, and each area has its own map of the opposite side of the body.
connects: It receives input from the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei and projects to the superior parietal lobule, supramarginal gyrus and precentral gyrus.
clinical: Damage causes loss of fine touch, proprioception, two-point discrimination, stereognosis and graphesthesia on the opposite side, with preserved strength.
remember: Postcentral lies behind the central sulcus: the precentral gyrus moves, the postcentral gyrus feels.
facts: It lies behind the central sulcus.
It contains Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2.
It is joined to the precentral gyrus at its two ends.

quiz.q: The long gyrus immediately behind the central sulcus, from the superior margin down to the lateral sulcus.
The gyrus bounded behind by the postcentral sulcus, continuous at its upper end with the paracentral lobule.

hint: ridge immediately ahead of the rolandic groove
summary: The precentral gyrus is the gyrus of the frontal lobe directly in front of the central sulcus, running from the superior margin to the lateral sulcus. It is the primary motor cortex, M1, and is bounded in front by the precentral sulcus. It receives input from the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus, premotor areas and somatosensory cortex. It gives rise to corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers that descend through the internal capsule.
where: The gyrus lies directly in front of the central sulcus, running from the superior margin to the lateral sulcus. It is bounded in front by the precentral sulcus, which has superior and inferior parts. At the top it merges with the paracentral lobule and at the bottom with the subcentral gyrus.
does: It is the primary motor cortex, M1. Its posterior part forms the anterior wall of the central sulcus. On axial MRI the hand region appears as an inverted omega-shaped knob of the gyrus bulging into the central sulcus, which is a reliable landmark for identifying the central sulcus.
connects: It receives input from the ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus, premotor areas and somatosensory cortex, and it sends corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers through the internal capsule.
clinical: Damage causes contralateral weakness or paralysis, with the pattern depending on the part of the homunculus involved. The gyrus is the main target of motor mapping in neurosurgery.
remember: Precentral lies in front of the central sulcus: the precentral gyrus moves, the postcentral gyrus feels.
facts: It lies in front of the central sulcus.
Its hand region forms the hand knob on axial MRI.
It is bounded in front by the precentral sulcus.

quiz.q: The long frontal gyrus directly in front of the central sulcus, bounded in front by the precentral sulcus.
The gyrus whose hand region appears as an inverted omega shaped knob on axial MRI, a landmark for the central sulcus.

hint: medial parietal surface in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus
summary: The precuneus is the quadrilateral medial surface of the parietal lobe. It is bounded in front by the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus, behind by the parieto-occipital sulcus and below by the subparietal sulcus, which separates it from the posterior cingulate. It is a hub of the default mode network with high resting metabolic activity. It takes part in visuospatial imagery, episodic memory retrieval, perspective taking and self-referential processing.
where: The precuneus is the quadrilateral medial surface of the parietal lobe. It is bounded in front by the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus, behind by the parieto-occipital sulcus and below by the subparietal sulcus, which separates it from the posterior cingulate. A medial view shows it best.
does: It takes part in visuospatial imagery, episodic memory retrieval, perspective taking and self-referential processing. It is a hub of the default mode network, with high resting metabolic activity. Its overall function remains debated.
connects: It is connected with the posterior cingulate, superior parietal lobule, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the lateral thalamic nuclei, and it sends fibers to premotor cortex and the basal ganglia.
clinical: It shows early amyloid deposition and reduced metabolism in Alzheimer disease. Bilateral damage may contribute to impairments of spatial attention and visuospatial imagery.
remember: Precuneus means before the wedge: it lies in front of the cuneus on the medial wall.
facts: It is on the medial parietal surface.
It lies in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.
It is a hub of the default mode network.

quiz.q: The quadrilateral medial parietal gyrus between the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus, above the subparietal sulcus.
The medial parietal gyrus active in visuospatial imagery, perspective taking and episodic memory retrieval.

hint: midline strip on the frontal underside beside the olfactory groove
summary: The gyrus rectus is a strip of cortex at the medial edge of the inferior frontal surface, running along the interhemispheric fissure medial to the olfactory sulcus. The olfactory bulb and tract lie in that sulcus. The gyrus forms part of ventromedial prefrontal and medial orbitofrontal cortex. It is connected with the amygdala, subcallosal area, mediodorsal thalamus and hypothalamus, and is associated with value-based decisions, emotion regulation and social behavior.
where: The gyrus is a strip of cortex at the medial edge of the inferior frontal surface, running along the interhemispheric fissure and medial to the olfactory sulcus. The olfactory bulb and tract lie in that sulcus. It is seen in an inferior or medial view.
does: It forms part of ventromedial prefrontal and medial orbitofrontal cortex. It is associated with value-based decisions, emotion regulation and social behavior. These functions are inferred mostly from imaging and lesion studies of the wider region.
connects: It is connected with the amygdala, the subcallosal area, the mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus and the hypothalamus, and with the adjacent olfactory pathways.
clinical: A ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm can bleed into the gyrus rectus, and neurosurgeons often resect part of it to reach the aneurysm. Ventromedial damage causes disinhibition and poor social judgment.
remember: Rectus means straight: this is the straight strip beside the midline.
facts: It lies medial to the olfactory sulcus.
It is on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
It is near the anterior communicating artery.

quiz.q: The straight strip of the inferior frontal surface between the interhemispheric fissure and the olfactory sulcus.
A ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm often produces a hematoma in this gyrus.

hint: small cortex beneath the front of the corpus callosum
summary: The subcallosal gyrus is a small area of cortex on the medial surface, below the rostrum and genu of the corpus callosum and in front of the lamina terminalis and anterior commissure. It includes the paraterminal gyrus and the parolfactory area and corresponds to the subgenual cingulate, around Brodmann area 25. It is connected with the amygdala, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex. It acts as a visceromotor and mood-regulating region that influences autonomic and endocrine responses to emotion.
where: The area lies on the medial surface below the rostrum and genu of the corpus callosum, in front of the lamina terminalis and anterior commissure. It includes the paraterminal gyrus and the parolfactory area, and it continues above into the anterior cingulate part. A midsagittal view shows it best.
does: It corresponds to the subgenual cingulate, around Brodmann area 25. It acts as a visceromotor and mood-regulating region, controlling autonomic and endocrine responses to emotion. It is overactive in depression in many imaging studies.
connects: It is connected with the amygdala, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, with output to autonomic and brainstem centers.
clinical: It is a target of deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression, although trial results are mixed. It also shows metabolic changes in mood disorders.
remember: Subcallosal means below the callosum: the area lies under the genu, just in front of the lamina terminalis.
facts: It lies below the genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum.
It is also called area 25.
It is a deep brain stimulation target for depression.

quiz.q: The small cortical area below the rostrum of the corpus callosum, in front of the lamina terminalis, also called the paraterminal gyrus.
The subgenual cortex around Brodmann area 25, a deep brain stimulation target for treatment-resistant depression.

hint: oblique ridge buried in the sylvian fissure on the temporal plane
summary: Heschl's gyrus, the anterior transverse temporal gyrus, is a ridge on the superior surface of the temporal lobe, hidden within the lateral sulcus. It runs obliquely from the retroinsular region toward the superior temporal gyrus, with the planum polare in front of it and the planum temporale behind it. It contains the core of the primary auditory cortex, A1, mainly in its medial two thirds. It receives auditory input from the medial geniculate nucleus through the auditory radiations.
where: The gyrus is a ridge on the superior surface of the temporal lobe, hidden within the lateral sulcus. It runs obliquely from the retroinsular region toward the superior temporal gyrus. The planum polare lies in front of it and the planum temporale behind it. It is seen in an opened sylvian fissure or on axial MRI.
does: It contains the core of the primary auditory cortex, A1, mainly in its medial two thirds, and tonotopic gradients run across it. Its shape varies: it can be single, partly duplicated or fully duplicated, and it is often asymmetric between hemispheres.
connects: It receives auditory input from the medial geniculate nucleus through the auditory radiations and projects to the surrounding auditory belt and parabelt regions.
clinical: Bilateral lesions can cause cortical deafness, and unilateral lesions cause subtle deficits in sound localization. Its volume and duplication patterns have been studied in relation to musical ability and to schizophrenia.
remember: Heschl's gyrus lies on the superior temporal plane between the two plana: polare in front, temporale behind.
facts: It is the anterior transverse temporal gyrus.
It is buried in the lateral sulcus.
It may be duplicated.

quiz.q: The oblique ridge on the superior temporal plane, with the planum polare in front and the planum temporale behind.
The transverse temporal gyrus whose shape varies as a single ridge or a duplicated one.

hint: uppermost ridge of the lobe below the sylvian fissure
summary: The superior temporal gyrus is the uppermost gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, forming the lower lip of the lateral sulcus and bounded below by the superior temporal sulcus. The Destrieux label covers its lateral aspect, while the surface hidden in the fissure is divided into Heschl's gyrus, the planum polare and the planum temporale. It contains auditory association cortex that processes complex sounds, including speech, voices and music. It receives input from primary auditory cortex and projects through the dorsal and ventral language pathways to frontal and parietal cortex.
where: The gyrus is the uppermost on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, forming the lower lip of the lateral sulcus and bounded below by the superior temporal sulcus. The Destrieux label covers the lateral aspect, while the surface hidden in the fissure is divided into Heschl's gyrus, the planum polare and the planum temporale. A lateral view shows it best.
does: It contains auditory association cortex that processes complex sounds, including speech, voices and music. The posterior part supports phonological and speech sound processing. The right side contributes to pitch and prosody.
connects: It receives input from primary auditory cortex and the medial geniculate nucleus, and it projects through the dorsal and ventral language pathways to frontal and parietal cortex.
clinical: Left posterior damage causes Wernicke's aphasia, with fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension. Right-sided damage can cause receptive aprosodia and amusia. Reduced volume has been reported in schizophrenia.
remember: T1: the first temporal gyrus, forming the lower lip of the sylvian fissure.
facts: It is the uppermost temporal gyrus.
It forms the lower lip of the lateral sulcus.
Left posterior damage causes Wernicke's aphasia.

quiz.q: The uppermost gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, forming the lower lip of the lateral sulcus.
Reduced volume of the left uppermost temporal gyrus has been reported in schizophrenia and linked to auditory hallucinations.

hint: flat floor of the sylvian fissure, ahead of the transverse ridge
summary: The planum polare is a flat, roughly triangular part of the superior temporal plane lying in front of Heschl's gyrus, inside the lateral sulcus. It points toward the temporal pole, which gives it its name. It is non-primary auditory association cortex, outside the primary auditory core. It is thought to belong to the anterior auditory stream, which is involved in sound identification, pitch and music processing.
where: The planum is a flat, roughly triangular part of the superior temporal plane lying in front of Heschl's gyrus, inside the lateral sulcus. It points toward the temporal pole. It is seen only when the fissure is opened, or in axial and coronal MRI.
does: It is non-primary auditory association cortex, outside the primary auditory core. It is thought to be part of the anterior auditory stream, involved in sound identification, pitch and music processing. Findings on its role are limited and mixed.
connects: It receives input from primary auditory cortex and belt areas and is connected with the anterior temporal lobe and the insula.
clinical: It has no well-defined syndrome of its own. It serves as a landmark for measuring the planum temporale and Heschl's gyrus, and its volume has been studied in some neurodevelopmental conditions.
remember: Polare refers to the pole: this is the part of the temporal plane in front of Heschl's gyrus, toward the temporal pole.
facts: It lies in front of Heschl's gyrus.
It is on the superior temporal plane.
It points toward the temporal pole.

quiz.q: The triangular surface of the superior temporal plane, in front of Heschl's gyrus.
The part of the superior temporal plane belonging to the anterior auditory stream, outside the primary auditory core.

hint: flat floor of the sylvian fissure behind the transverse ridge
summary: The planum temporale is a flat, triangular part of the superior temporal plane lying behind Heschl's gyrus and forming the floor of the lateral sulcus. It extends back toward the inferior parietal lobule. It processes the spectral and temporal structure of sounds and takes part in auditory-motor integration for speech. It is a classic example of structural asymmetry, being larger on the left in most people.
where: The planum is a flat, triangular part of the superior temporal plane lying behind Heschl's gyrus, forming the floor of the lateral sulcus. It extends back toward the inferior parietal lobule and is seen in an opened fissure or on axial MRI. The 3D outline of Wernicke's area is drawn on it as an approximation, since Wernicke's area itself extends into the posterior superior and middle temporal gyri.
does: It processes the spectral and temporal structure of sounds and takes part in auditory-motor integration for speech and in the localization of sound. It is a classic example of structural asymmetry, being larger on the left in most people.
connects: It receives input from Heschl's gyrus and the auditory belt and is connected with the supramarginal gyrus and the frontal lobe through the arcuate fasciculus.
clinical: Asymmetry was first demonstrated in post-mortem brains by Geschwind and Levitsky. Reduced asymmetry has been reported in dyslexia and schizophrenia, although results are inconsistent. A larger left planum temporale has been linked to absolute pitch.
remember: Temporale lies behind Heschl's gyrus: planum polare in front, planum temporale behind, and the left one is larger.
facts: It is larger on the left in most people.
It lies behind Heschl's gyrus.
It was shown asymmetric by Geschwind and Levitsky.

quiz.q: The flat triangular area on the upper surface of the temporal lobe behind Heschl's gyrus.
The classic example of structural asymmetry in the brain, reported by Geschwind and Levitsky as larger on the left.

hint: lowest lateral ridge of the lobe beside the ear, wraps underneath
summary: The inferior temporal gyrus is the lowest gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus. It wraps around the inferolateral edge onto the inferior surface and ends at the occipitotemporal sulcus beside the fusiform gyrus. It constitutes inferotemporal cortex, the final stage of the ventral visual stream, where neurons are selective for complex objects, faces and categories. It receives input from V4 and the fusiform region and projects to perirhinal and entorhinal cortex, the amygdala and prefrontal cortex.
where: The gyrus is the lowest on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus. It wraps around the inferolateral edge onto the inferior surface, ending at the occipitotemporal sulcus beside the fusiform gyrus. A lateral or inferior view shows it best.
does: It is inferotemporal cortex, the final stage of the ventral visual stream, where neurons are selective for complex objects, faces and categories. On the left it also takes part in semantic memory and word retrieval.
connects: It receives input from V4 and the fusiform region and projects to perirhinal and entorhinal cortex, the amygdala and prefrontal cortex.
clinical: Damage can cause visual agnosia, prosopagnosia or category-specific naming deficits. It is often involved in temporal lobe epilepsy and in the atrophy of semantic dementia.
remember: T3: the lowest of the three lateral temporal gyri and the final stage of object recognition.
facts: It lies below the inferior temporal sulcus.
It is the end of the ventral visual stream.
It wraps onto the inferior surface.

quiz.q: The lowest gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus, wrapping onto the underside.
Cortex at the end of the ventral visual stream whose neurons are selective for complex objects and faces.

hint: ridge between the two long grooves on the side of the lobe
summary: The middle temporal gyrus lies on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe between the superior temporal sulcus above and the inferior temporal sulcus below. It runs from the temporal pole back toward the occipital lobe, where it merges with the lateral occipital region. Its left posterior part supports word meaning, lexical retrieval and sentence comprehension. Its posterior end near the occipital border, which includes motion area MT, processes visual motion.
where: The gyrus lies on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe between the superior temporal sulcus above and the inferior temporal sulcus below. It runs from the temporal pole back toward the occipital lobe, where it merges with the lateral occipital region. A lateral view shows it best.
does: The left posterior part supports word meaning, lexical retrieval and sentence comprehension. Its posterior end near the occipital border, which includes motion area MT, processes visual motion. Many other functions, such as biological motion and face perception, have been reported.
connects: It is connected with the inferior frontal gyrus through the ventral language pathway, the extreme capsule and the arcuate fasciculus, and with the anterior temporal lobe.
clinical: Left posterior damage causes word-finding and comprehension problems and can produce transcortical sensory aphasia with preserved repetition. The gyrus shows early atrophy in Alzheimer disease and in semantic dementia.
remember: T2: the middle temporal gyrus lies between the two sulci, the middle of three stacked lateral gyri.
facts: It lies between the superior and inferior temporal sulci.
It is also called T2.
Left posterior damage can cause transcortical sensory aphasia.

quiz.q: The gyrus on the lateral temporal surface between the superior temporal sulcus and the inferior temporal sulcus.
Left posterior damage here can cause poor comprehension and word finding with preserved repetition (transcortical sensory aphasia).

hint: rear tip of the brain, where central vision is mapped
summary: The occipital pole is the posterior tip of the occipital lobe and the most posterior point of the hemisphere. The calcarine sulcus ends near it. It represents central vision, with the fovea mapped where V1, V2 and V3 meet at the foveal confluence. A large amount of cortex is devoted to the small central region of the visual field, and the pole receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the optic radiation.
where: The pole is the posterior tip of the occipital lobe, the most posterior point of the hemisphere. The calcarine sulcus ends near it. It is seen in a posterior view or at the back of a sagittal view.
does: It represents central vision. The fovea is mapped here, where V1, V2 and V3 meet at the foveal confluence, and a large amount of cortex is devoted to the small central region of the visual field.
connects: It receives input from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the optic radiation and projects to V2 and other extrastriate areas.
clinical: Its blood supply is shared by the posterior and middle cerebral arteries, so macular sparing is seen after a posterior cerebral artery stroke. A lesion of the pole alone causes a contralateral central scotoma. Trauma to the back of the head causes coup injury here and contrecoup contusion of the frontal poles.
remember: The pole is the tip, and the tip represents the center of the visual field: the fovea is mapped at the occipital pole.
facts: It represents the fovea.
It has a dual blood supply from the PCA and MCA.
It is the most posterior point of the cortex.

quiz.q: The most posterior tip of the occipital lobe, the point opposite the frontal pole.
The tip of the occipital lobe where the foveal representation lies, explaining macular sparing after a posterior cerebral artery stroke.

hint: front tip of the lobe, tucked against the sphenoid wing
summary: The temporal pole is the anterior tip of the temporal lobe and corresponds to Brodmann area 38. It lies in the middle cranial fossa behind the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, below the anterior end of the lateral sulcus. It is an anterior temporal hub for semantic knowledge, especially about people, places and social concepts. It is connected with the orbitofrontal cortex through the uncinate fasciculus, with the amygdala and with the inferior and middle temporal gyri.
where: The pole is the anterior tip of the temporal lobe, corresponding to Brodmann area 38. It lies in the middle cranial fossa behind the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, below the anterior end of the lateral sulcus. It is seen in lateral or inferior views.
does: It is an anterior temporal hub for semantic knowledge, especially about people, places and social concepts, and it links high-level sensory input with emotion. It also takes part in the retrieval of person-specific memories and in social cognition. Its exact function remains debated.
connects: It is connected with the orbitofrontal cortex through the uncinate fasciculus, with the amygdala and with the inferior and middle temporal gyri.
clinical: Bilateral anterior temporal atrophy causes semantic dementia, with loss of word and object meaning and fluent speech. Anterior temporal lobectomy treats drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy and can damage Meyer's loop, causing a superior quadrantanopia. Bilateral damage including the amygdala can produce Kluver-Bucy syndrome.
remember: Pole means tip: the temporal pole is the anterior tip of the lobe and a hub for the meaning of things and people.
facts: It corresponds to Brodmann area 38.
It is connected with the orbitofrontal cortex by the uncinate fasciculus.
It is the site of atrophy in semantic dementia.

quiz.q: The anterior tip of the temporal lobe, lying in the middle cranial fossa behind the greater wing of the sphenoid.
Progressive loss of the meaning of words and objects with fluent speech (semantic dementia) is linked with atrophy of this tip of the lobe.
